summary: Specifies how to use the Session Description Protocol to describe the configuration of the FEC Framework between sender and receiver. It includes examples of grouping multiple source and repair flows.

plainLanguage.summary: Before using error-fixing extras, both sides must agree on the settings. This explains how to write those settings in the standard description language used to set up calls and streams.

questions: how to describe fec in sdp
what is the sdp repair-window attribute
subtitle: How to write down the settings of a Forward Error Correction setup using SDP session descriptions.

tldr.problem: The FEC Framework needs a set of parameters shared between sender and receiver, such as which flows carry source and repair packets and which FEC scheme is used, but it does not say how to encode them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6364 encodes those parameters in the Session Description Protocol, using two new transport protocol identifiers and three new attributes (fec-source-flow, fec-repair-flow and repair-window), plus existing grouping and bandwidth attributes.
tldr.outcome: Senders can announce or negotiate FEC protection options in ordinary SDP, including cases with several source and repair flows. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 6364 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2011, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the framework in RFC 6363.

sections.title: Why FEC Needs SDP
sections.content:
The Forward Error Correction (FEC) Framework in RFC 6363 describes how to protect packet flows carrying media with FEC. A Content Delivery Protocol (CDP) that uses it does not need continuous signaling between sender and receiver. It does need a set of parameters communicated once at the start, and a signaling protocol is required to carry them.

One format for those parameters is the Session Description Protocol (SDP) from RFC 4566, a simple text-based format for announcements and invitations to multimedia sessions. SDP also offers a framework for capability negotiation. RFC 6364 introduces the SDP elements for CDPs that choose SDP.
sections.plainLanguage: Two friends who want to play a game over a walkie-talkie first agree on the rules. SDP is the standard note used to write down such rules for streams, and this document adds the lines needed for error repair.

sections.title: FEC and the FEC Framework
sections.content:
FEC groups source packets into blocks and applies protection to generate a desired number of repair packets. It is especially useful for multicast and broadcast, where receiver feedback is unavailable or limited. Repair packets can be sent on demand or independently of feedback. At the receiver, lost packets can be recovered by erasure decoding if enough source and repair packets arrive.

The framework defines the common parts of CDPs and the requirements for FEC schemes, but not how repair packets are generated or how configuration information is communicated. Those details belong to the individual FEC schemes or CDPs.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine sending a puzzle in the mail with a few spare pieces added. If one piece is lost on the way, the spares let the receiver fill the gap without asking for a resend.

sections.title: FEC Framework Configuration Information
sections.content:
The framework defines a minimum set called the FEC Framework Configuration Information that sender and receivers must share. Each instance of the framework provides:

  • the identification of the repair flows;
  • for each protected source flow, its definition and an integer identifier that MUST be unique among all source flows protected by the same repair flow;
  • the FEC Encoding ID, which identifies the FEC scheme;
  • the length of the Explicit Source FEC Payload ID in octets;
  • zero or more FEC-Scheme-Specific Information (FSSI) elements, each a name and a value defined by the FEC scheme.

FSSI needed only by the sender travels in the Sender-Side FSSI (SS-FSSI) container. This lets a receiver or a third party control FEC at the sender. Any other FSSI MUST go in the FSSI container. Multiple framework instances can exist at the same time for different source flows, the same source flow, or combinations of them.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a checklist: which streams carry the data, which streams carry the spare pieces, which repair method is used, and any extra settings that method needs.

sections.title: The New SDP Attributes
sections.content:
Two new transport protocol identifiers are defined. FEC/UDP is for schemes that take a UDP-formatted input stream and append an Explicit Source FEC Payload ID. For other transports, a matching FEC/<proto> identifier MUST be registered with IANA. If a scheme does not use the Explicit Source FEC Payload ID, the original transport identifier MUST be kept for backward compatibility with receivers that do not support FEC. UDP/FEC marks the FEC repair packet format of RFC 6363.

The attribute a=fec-source-flow identifies a source flow. Its required id parameter is an integer. The tag-len parameter gives the length of the Explicit Source FEC Payload ID in octets. It MUST be present if such an ID is used and MUST NOT be present otherwise.

The attribute a=fec-repair-flow describes a repair flow, which MUST carry only repair packets for a single framework instance. Its parameters are:

  • encoding-id (required): the FEC scheme, in the range 0 to 255, registered by the schemes and maintained by IANA;
  • preference-lvl (optional): the preferred order for using repair flows. Without it, receivers MAY use the flows in any order;
  • ss-fssi and fssi (optional): the sender-side and other FSSI containers. If the scheme needs no specific information, they MUST NOT be present.
sections.plainLanguage: Each stream gets a name tag. Data streams say "I am number 0", and repair streams say which repair method they use and, if needed, in what order to prefer them.

sections.title: Repair Window, Grouping and Bandwidth
sections.content:
The repair window is the time spanned by a FEC block, meaning the source block plus its repair packets. The sender transmits all of them within a duration not larger than the window. The receiver should wait at least that long after the first packet of a block before concluding anything, and SHOULD NOT register a FEC decoding failure sooner. The new media-level attribute a=repair-window gives the size as a number followed by ms (milliseconds) or us (microseconds).

Existing SDP features do the rest. Source and repair flows are associated with the group attribute and the FEC grouping semantics of RFC 5888 and RFC 5956. Source addresses use the source-filter attribute of RFC 4570. For bandwidth, TIAS (RFC 3890) with a=maxprate is RECOMMENDED, and the AS modifier is NOT RECOMMENDED because TIAS allows the bitrate to be calculated according to the IP version and transport protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The repair window is how long you wait for stragglers. If some of the puzzle pieces are late, you hold on a bit before deciding you cannot finish the picture.

sections.title: Announcements, Offer/Answer and Examples
sections.content:
In multicast use, a sender MAY announce every FEC protection option as part of the session announcement. Receivers choose one or more framework instances and join the matching multicast sessions. Unless the CDP requires it, receivers SHOULD NOT send an answer, because that can overwhelm the sender in large deployments.

In unicast use, sender and receiver MAY use the Offer/Answer Model of RFC 3264: the sender offers the options available to that receiver, and the receiver answers with its choice. The SDP Capability Negotiation Framework of RFC 5939 MAY also be used.

Section 6 gives four scenarios: one source flow with one repair flow, two source flows with one repair flow, two source flows with two repair flows and two schemes, and one source flow with two repair flows and two schemes. Using the same values for mid and for source flow identifiers is NOT RECOMMENDED. The examples use random FEC Encoding IDs and artificial FSSI content for illustration.
sections.plainLanguage: For a big broadcast, the sender just posts a menu and nobody has to reply. For a one-to-one call, the two sides trade offers until they agree.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC calls the threat weak. If SDP is altered to show a wrong association or grouping of source and repair flows, FEC protection can fail or other media streams can be mishandled. Receivers are RECOMMENDED to perform an integrity check on SDP and trust it only from trusted sources. They MUST also follow the security considerations of RFC 4566. The security considerations of the FEC Framework in RFC 6363 also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone sneaks a wrong note into the rules, the repair streams may not match the data streams. So only trust notes that come from someone you trust.

viz.caption: ABNF OF THE REPAIR FLOW ATTRIBUTE (RFC 6364)

data.title: fec-repair-flow
data.code:
fec-repair-flow-line = "a=fec-repair-flow:" SP fec-encoding-id
     [";" SP flow-preference]
     [";" SP sender-side-scheme-specific]
     [";" SP scheme-specific] CRLF

fec-encoding-id = "encoding-id=" enc-id
flow-preference = "preference-lvl=" preference-level-of-the-flow
sender-side-scheme-specific = "ss-fssi=" sender-info
scheme-specific = "fssi=" scheme-info

viz.caption: EXAMPLE SDP, ONE SOURCE FLOW AND ONE REPAIR FLOW (RFC 6364)

data.title: Scenario 1
data.code:
v=0
o=ali 1122334455 1122334466 IN IP4 fec.example.com
s=FEC Framework Examples
t=0 0
a=group:FEC-FR S1 R1
m=video 30000 RTP/AVP 100
c=IN IP4 233.252.0.1/127
a=rtpmap:100 MP2T/90000
a=fec-source-flow: id=0
a=mid:S1
m=application 30000 UDP/FEC
c=IN IP4 233.252.0.2/127
a=fec-repair-flow: encoding-id=0; ss-fssi=n:7,k:5
a=repair-window:150ms
a=mid:R1
